opus-5.5.text:
I think the choice is actually quite natural if you look at what Kimi Linear is trying to claim. The core message of that work is: can a hybrid linear attention architecture, with something like three linear layers to one full attention layer, match or even beat a full attention baseline under a fair, controlled setting? Full attention is still the default that everyone ships in production. So if you want to convince people to switch, the baseline you have to beat is the thing they're already using, not another alternative that most teams haven't adopted yet.

Sparse attention is a somewhat different line of work. Methods like DeepSeek's NSA or DSA are mostly about making full attention cheaper at inference by selecting which tokens to attend to. They still keep a KV cache that grows with sequence length, so the memory story is different. Linear attention, or more precisely these gated delta-rule style recurrent layers, compresses history into a fixed-size state. They solve overlapping but not identical problems, so a head-to-head comparison isn't always apples to apples. You'd have to decide whether you're comparing on quality, on decoding throughput, on KV cache memory, or on long-context retrieval, and the answer can flip depending on which axis you pick.

There's also a practical side. Running a really fair comparison at scale is expensive. Every extra baseline means another full pretraining run with matched data and compute, and sparse attention methods often have a lot of system-level details, kernels, block sizes, selection strategies, that make it easy to under-tune someone else's method. Comparing against a well-tuned full attention model is the cleanest and most credible thing you can do.

And honestly, I don't see them as competitors in the long run. Sparse attention and linear attention are quite complementary. You could imagine a hybrid where the linear layers handle local and compressed global information cheaply, and the few remaining global layers use sparse attention instead of dense attention. That's probably where things are heading. So comparing against full attention first establishes that the linear part holds up, and then combining with sparsity is a natural next step rather than an either-or.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the comparison choice comes down to what question you're actually trying to answer. Kimi Linear is a hybrid architecture, so the real question isn't "is linear attention better than some other efficiency trick," it's "can we replace full attention without losing anything." Full attention is the gold standard that everyone trusts. If you only compare against sparse attention, you're comparing two approximations to each other, and a skeptical reader will say, well, maybe you're both just worse than the real thing. Beating full attention at matched compute, on the same data, with the same training recipe, is the cleanest evidence that the design is actually sound.

There's also a practical reason. Sparse attention methods like DSA or NSA involve a lot of design choices—block sizes, selection mechanisms, which layers get sparsified—and the results depend heavily on those details and on the specific implementation. It's hard to set up a fair head-to-head where nobody can argue about the baseline. Full attention has essentially no hyperparameters to argue about. It's a fixed target.

And honestly, I'd say linear attention and sparse attention aren't really competitors in the way people sometimes frame them. They attack the long-context problem from different angles. Linear attention compresses history into a fixed-size state, which gives you constant memory and very fast decoding. Sparse attention keeps the full KV cache but only reads part of it, so you keep precise retrieval over very long ranges. In a hybrid model those can coexist—you could imagine a mix of KDA layers with a sparse global attention layer instead of a dense one. So the Kimi Linear paper is really asking a more fundamental question: how much of the model's attention budget can you hand to a linear mechanism, and does the model get better or worse. Full attention is the right baseline for that question. Comparing against sparse attention would be a different paper, and probably a follow-up worth doing.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: why use Full Attention as the baseline, and whether that comparison is sufficient. Full Attention gives you a straightforward reference for the quality and cost tradeoff: how much computation and memory can you save, and what happens to model quality?

Sparse Attention is also an important comparison, but it introduces another set of choices—which tokens to attend to, how to select them, and how efficiently that selection runs. There isn’t one configuration that represents all Sparse Attention methods.

So I’d interpret the Full Attention comparison as establishing a baseline, not as demonstrating that Kimi Linear is better than Sparse Attention. To make that stronger claim, you’d need a matched comparison with competitive sparse methods. I can explain that rationale, but I wouldn’t claim it was the team’s actual motivation without more information.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is what question we’re trying to answer. Full attention is the natural reference point if we want to ask: can a linear-attention architecture improve efficiency while preserving the model’s capabilities? Comparing against full attention makes that tradeoff clearer.

Sparse attention is also an important comparison, but it introduces another set of choices: which tokens attend to which others, how much sparsity you use, and whether the pattern changes across layers. Those choices affect both quality and speed, so there isn’t one universal sparse-attention baseline.

That doesn’t mean a comparison with sparse attention is unnecessary. If we’re asking which architecture is best for a particular deployment, we should compare strong implementations of both under the same conditions. But full attention provides a clear starting point for evaluating whether the linear approach itself works.
